content: The level of hepatitis C virus (HCV) prevalence in the survey year was comparable to the annual changes observed in the United States between their two surveys. Detailed methodological information, including the calibration methods and model equations for each submodel, is provided in the supplementary materials. To assess the number of HCV infections averted (IA) per treatment over 13 and 20 years starting from 2017, full model simulations for each country were initially run through 2037 without any treatments. This counterfactual projection estimated the number of new infections occurring between 2017 and 2037. Subsequently, the same models were run with 1,000 individuals treated in 2017, and the number of new infections over the same period was compared to the counterfactual projections. The IA and IA per treatment were calculated by dividing the difference by 1,000. Scenarios assumed that the 1,000 treated individuals were either randomly selected from the entire infected population or specifically chosen from subgroups such as people who inject drugs (PWID), individuals with cirrhosis, or infected individuals over 30 years of age. Regional and global estimates of IA per treatment were derived by weighting country-level estimates based on each country’s relative HCV burden compared to regional and global burdens. Multivariable regression models were employed to investigate which country-level characteristics (e.g., predicted population growth from 2015 to 2040, the population-attributable fraction (PAF) of injection drug use (IDU) to HCV transmission, prevalence of IDU among adults, average duration of IDU, and HCV prevalence among PWID and the general population) were associated with the number of IA per randomly allocated treatment and per treatment for infected PWID. The PAF of IDU to HCV transmission was estimated as the percentage of new HCV infections that would be prevented from 2017 to 2037 if the transmission risk due to IDU were eliminated during this period. To evaluate the effect of temporal dynamics of the HCV epidemic on the number of IA per treatment, a second multivariable regression model was used. This model analyzed each of the 20 runs per country and treated the country as a random effect. The same variables as above were included, along with the yearly percentage change in HCV prevalence in the general population between 2037 and the year when a general population HCV prevalence estimate was available. The model successfully ran for 82 out of 83 countries, with Seychelles being the exception due to a lower estimated HCV burden in the general population compared to the prevalence burden among current PWID. The modeling covered countries representing 84% of the global population. It was estimated that 4 million people would become chronically infected with HCV from 2017 to 2037. The IA per treatment over the next 20 years from treating people randomly varied widely across regions, with substantial variation even within regions. The prevention benefit of targeting treatment to different groups of infected individuals was analyzed. For example, targeting PWID could yield a greater impact, with over one infection averted on average for each PWID treated. However, this varied significantly by region, with negative infections averted in 15 of 82 modeled countries but up to 3.7 infections prevented per PWID treated in sub-Saharan Africa. In 68% of the modeled countries, treating PWID would prevent more infections than randomly allocating treatment, while the opposite was true in the remaining countries. Country-level differences in the prevention impact achieved from either treating PWID or randomly allocating treatment were strongly related to the country’s population growth rate. More infections were prevented in settings with higher population growth, such as Pakistan and Afghanistan, while fewer infections were prevented in settings with significant HCV epidemics among PWID. The prevalence of HCV among PWID was a strong negative predictor of impact. The importance of IDU in driving HCV transmission also influenced the impact of randomly allocated treatment, with less impact achieved in settings where IDU was the primary contributor to transmission. The modeling’s strength lies in its simulation of a wide range of country-level HCV epidemics, covering most of the world’s population (84%). It accounted for the differing roles of PWID in each HCV epidemic and variations in population demographics and growth. However, data limitations meant that over half of the world’s countries, predominantly lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), were not represented, potentially affecting regional and global results. The modeling required a generalizable structure and standardized algorithm for fitting the model to each country’s epidemic, which posed challenges in some cases, particularly due to the lack of data on population migration. Migration could be a significant source of new HCV infections in some countries, potentially affecting the prevention benefits of treatment. The lack of high-quality data on the prevalence of PWID, HCV in the general population, and HCV among PWID in most countries was a major limitation. Additionally, there was limited information on the evolving HCV epidemic for most countries, with only three countries (Egypt, France, and the USA) having robust data on changes in HCV prevalence over time. This uncertainty in the temporal dynamics of country-level HCV epidemics was incorporated into the model runs. The findings emphasize the importance of improving country-level information on the ongoing trajectory of HCV epidemics to better estimate the likely impact of scaling up treatment. This study is the first to consider the prevention benefit of different HCV treatment allocation strategies across country settings, produce a global estimate for infections averted per treatment, and evaluate which country-level factors affect the achieved impact. The analyses show that globally, a moderate prevention impact (one infection prevented per two treatments) can be achieved with a treat-all strategy, although this varies depending on country-level factors. These findings are valuable for policymakers as they provide a better understanding of the prevention benefits of widespread treatment when planning for the WHO 2030 HCV elimination targets. LMICs are likely to achieve greater prevention benefits due to growing populations and generalized epidemics, highlighting that scaling up treatment could be more cost-effective in these settings. However, many LMICs may lack the resources to treat HCV, and screening may present a barrier to treatment scale-up due to the generalized nature of their HCV epidemics. Substantial donor support or significant reductions in the costs of HCV drugs and diagnostic tests will be necessary for such countries to scale up treatment. The analyses underscore the prevention benefits of targeting PWID, which is the most effective treatment strategy globally and in many countries. This is due to their higher likelihood of transmitting HCV to others compared to other subgroups. However, PWID represent only a fraction of the overall HCV burden, so any elimination strategy would also need to target other groups. In settings where HCV prevalence among PWID is high (chronic HCV prevalence exceeds 50%), moderate levels of treatment among PWID do not avert infections due to their high likelihood of reinfection. In such settings, treatment rates among PWID must be high to overcome this issue, or other HCV prevention interventions for PWID (e.g., needle and syringe programs or opioid substitution therapy) need to be scaled up to sufficiently reduce the chance of reinfection. These findings emphasize the need to allocate resources to treating PWID, either due to the greater prevention benefits achieved or to gain control of the epidemic among PWID, which will be crucial for achieving elimination. For preventing infection, the findings support a change in WHO guidelines towards a treat-all strategy, with special emphasis on treating PWID. Such a strategy would reduce practical obstacles to treatment, such as screening to identify individuals with advanced disease, and could be considered more equitable by allowing all those who seek treatment to access it. While cost considerations and resource prioritization remain challenges, if these can be overcome, a widespread treat-all strategy will achieve considerable prevention benefits in most settings and should be advocated.
